kaps_punt: Die leefwyse in die antieke Egipte: Opvattings en godsdiens; Sosiale struktuur in antieke Egipte

items.bewering: Die meeste kos het van die landerye langs die Nyl gekom.
items.bron: Harvard Giza Project, 'Social Status in Ancient Egypt' (giza.fas.harvard.edu): Egypt was an agricultural society and most people were peasant farmers; Fitzwilliam Museum fact sheet 'Food and farming' (schools.fitzmuseum.cam.ac.uk): the diet rested on grain grown in the Nile valley. 'Die meeste' is a quantifier, not 'alle'. Fish and wildfowl came from the river and marsh, which the lesson itself says later, so the quantifier is right.

items.bewering: Brood en bier was die stapelvoedsel van ryk en arm mense.
items.bron: Fitzwilliam Museum fact sheet 'Food and farming'; Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Food and Feasts in Middle Kingdom Egypt' (metmuseum.org): bread, mostly from emmer wheat, and beer were the base of the diet for rich and poor alike, and beer was drunk by men, women and children as nourishment.

items.bewering: Wat op die landerye gegroei het: koring en gars
items.blok: Wat op die landerye gegroei het
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Food & Drink in Ancient Egypt' (worldhistory.org/article/2494); Met, 'Food and Feasts in Middle Kingdom Egypt': emmer wheat and barley were the main grains, for bread and beer. 'Koring' for the emmer wheat Egypt grew is a fair simplification.

items.bewering: Wat op die landerye gegroei het: uie en blaarslaai
items.blok: Wat op die landerye gegroei het
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Food & Drink in Ancient Egypt': onions, garlic and radishes were grown, along with salad crops such as lettuce; lettuce also appears in offering scenes and is linked to the god Min.

items.bewering: Wat op die landerye gegroei het: dadels, vye en druiwe
items.blok: Wat op die landerye gegroei het
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Food & Drink in Ancient Egypt': dates were the commonest fruit; sycamore figs and common figs were grown; grapes were eaten fresh and made into wine, though they grew less easily than elsewhere and wine was a luxury. Note only: dates, figs and grapes grew on trees and vines in orchards and gardens rather than in fields in the narrow sense of 'landerye'; read as 'farmland' the heading holds.

items.bewering: In die warm Egipte het mense ligte klere van linne gedra.
items.bron: Iziko Museums of South Africa, 'Clothing and adornment of ancient Egypt' (egyptinsouthafrica.iziko.org.za): most Egyptians wore clothing made from linen from the flax plant, a fabric that is cool and comfortable to wear.

items.bewering: Linne is 'n stof wat van die vlasplant gemaak word.
items.bron: Iziko Museums of South Africa, 'Clothing and adornment of ancient Egypt'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Cloth Production': linen is made from flax fibres separated from the stem, spun and woven.

items.bewering: Klere en juwele het iemand se plek in die samelewing gewys.
items.bron: Iziko Museums of South Africa, 'Clothing and adornment of ancient Egypt': clothing signalled status, wealthier people had more elaborate garments and only the rich could afford brightly coloured cloth; jewellery was worn at every level but its richness varied. Ancient Egypt Online, 'Clothing': a man's rank showed in how elaborate his kilt was and how fine its linen.

items.bewering: Die meeste mense was boere.
items.bron: Harvard Giza Project, 'Social Status in Ancient Egypt': as an agricultural society, most people were peasant farmers. Royal Ontario Museum (rom.on.ca): the great mass of people worked on the land. Note only: many worked land owned by the state, temples or officials, but they were still farmers, so 'boere' holds.

items.bewering: Vakmanne het potte, meubels en gereedskap gemaak.
items.bron: Accounts of the craftsmen's village of Deir el-Medina (Michigan State University DAEA site entry; exploreluxor.org 'Artisans of ancient Egypt'): the village was served by carpenters, potters and coppersmiths, who made pottery, furniture and metal tools.

items.bewering: Mense het met musiek, dans en speletjies ontspan.
items.bron: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Female Musicians' (collection 557727) and the Met facsimile catalogue 'Drink and be merry' (2019): music and dance were part of festivals, banquets and processions; Met essay 'Ancient Egypt board games': board games were played by royalty and ordinary people.

items.bewering: Senet was 'n gewilde bordspeletjie waarin twee spelers hulle stukke oor 'n bord geskuif het.
items.bron: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Ancient Egypt board games' (metmuseum.org/perspectives/ancient-egypt-board-games) and 'Board Games from Ancient Egypt and the Near East': senet is the best-known Egyptian game, in favour from the Predynastic to at least the Late Period; two players moved pieces along a board of 30 squares, using casting sticks or knucklebones; queens played on game boxes and poorer Egyptians on grids scratched into floors, so 'gewilde' holds.

items.bewering: Kinders het ook speletjies gespeel en speelgoed gehad.
items.bron: World History Encyclopedia, 'Games, Sports & Recreation in Ancient Egypt' (worldhistory.org/article/1036): children's toys included balls filled with seeds, spinning tops, carved animals, wooden dolls and pull-toys; children's games such as ball games, wrestling and juggling are shown in tomb scenes.

items.bewering: Die Egiptenare het in baie gode geglo, soos die songod Ra en Anubis, die god van mummifisering.
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Re' (britannica.com/topic/Re): Re (Ra), the god of the sun and a creator god, within a religion of many gods. Western Australian Museum, Afterlife exhibition, curator's introduction 'Anubis' (museum.wa.gov.au), drawing on British Museum material: as the god 'who is in the embalming tent' Anubis oversees mummification. Anubis was also a god of cemeteries and the dead, but 'die god van mummifisering' is the standard short description.

items.bewering: Mense het by tempels gebid en offers soos kos en drinkgoed gebring.
items.bron: Wikipedia, 'Ancient Egyptian offerings', citing Ockinga, 'Piety', in Redford (ed.), Oxford Encyclopedia of Ancient Egypt (2001), and UCL Digital Egypt 'Daily cult': individual Egyptians prayed to gods and gave them private offerings; food, drink, clothing and ointment were offered to deities. Temple 'chapels of the hearing ear' let ordinary people address the god at the temple wall (Kom Ombo marker, hmdb.org; Swedish museum object record, collections.smvk.se). Note for the person reviewing, not a fault: ordinary people did not enter a temple's inner rooms, so the lesson's 'by tempels' (at temples, not in them) is the accurate preposition and should not be changed to 'in tempels'. The commonest private gift was often a small object such as a statuette or stela; the daily food-and-drink offering inside the temple was made by priests.

items.bewering: Baie het ook amulette vir beskerming gedra.
items.bron: Johns Hopkins Archaeological Museum, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets' (archaeologicalmuseum.jhu.edu): amulets protected the living as well as the dead. Iziko Museums of South Africa, 'Clothing and adornment of ancient Egypt': the main purpose of ornaments was protection against evil forces.

items.bewering: In daardie tyd het seuns dikwels hulle pa se werk geleer.
items.blok: Leer by die huis en op skool
items.bron: Zinn, 'Education, Pharaonic Egypt' (University of Wales Trinity Saint David repository, repository.uwtsd.ac.uk/566): most boys learned their father's occupation on the job, and fathers are known to have trained their own sons, including in scribal skills.

items.bewering: Meisies het dikwels by hulle ma geleer om brood te bak en linne te weef.
items.blok: Leer by die huis en op skool
items.bron: Grinding grain and baking were household work done by women in nearly every home ('Maids at the grindstone', Journal of Lithic Studies, University of Edinburgh); most textile workers were women and nearly every home had spinning and weaving space (Encyclopedia.com, 'Cloth Production'); girls were mostly taught at home by their mothers (World History Encyclopedia, 'The Gifts of Isis: Women's Status in Ancient Egypt'; Girl Museum, 'A Girl in Ancient Egypt'). The mother-to-daughter transmission rests on general-reference sources, but it follows directly from the scholarly evidence that these were women's household tasks, and 'dikwels' is correctly hedged; in the New Kingdom men also wove on vertical looms in workshops, which 'dikwels' accommodates.

items.bewering: Net sommige kinders het skoolgegaan, veral uit ryk families en dikwels om skrifgeleerdes te word.
items.blok: Leer by die huis en op skool
items.bron: Zinn, 'Education, Pharaonic Egypt' (UWTSD repository): the scribal school is the best-documented form of education; boys chosen were usually sons of scribes, priests and officials, and most children never attended school; there was no formal class bar, which the lesson's 'veral' correctly allows for.

items.bewering: Min mense kon lees en skryf.
items.blok: Leer by die huis en op skool
items.bron: UCL Digital Egypt, 'Literacy' (ucl.ac.uk/museums-static/digitalegypt/literature/literacy.html): estimates range from about 1 to 5 percent of the population (Baines and Eyre), possibly higher in towns. 'Min' holds on any of these estimates.

items.bewering: 'n Boer se gesin het minder gereeld vleis geëet as 'n ryk familie.
items.bron: Fitzwilliam Museum fact sheet 'Food and farming': only the rich could afford to eat beef regularly; the average Egyptian relied on fish and wildfowl. History Hit, 'The Diet of the Nile': poor Egyptians ate meat on special occasions.

items.bewering: Vis uit die Nyl was vir 'n boer se gesin belangrik.
items.bron: Fitzwilliam Museum fact sheet 'Food and farming': the average ancient Egyptian relied on fish and wildfowl for protein; ICSF, 'Egypt: Fisheries history': fish was a cheap source of protein for ordinary people. Some priests and elites avoided certain fish, which does not affect a claim about farming families.

items.bewering: 'n Boer se klere was eenvoudig, maar ryk mense het fyn linne en goue juwele gedra.
items.bron: Iziko Museums of South Africa, 'Clothing and adornment of ancient Egypt': labourers wore linen loincloths or nothing at all, while wealthier people had more elaborate garments; gold was the colour of the gods. Ancient Egypt Online, 'Clothing': very fine, almost sheer linen for the wealthy and coarse cloth for labourers. This sits consistently with the earlier block: farmers also wore linen, just coarse and plain.

items.bewering: Vandag gaan die meeste kinders skool, en baie meer mense kan lees en skryf.
items.bron: United Nations, Sustainable Development Goals Extended Report 2026, Goal 4 (unstats.un.org): the out-of-school rate for children and youth was 16.8 percent in 2024, so most attend; 754 million adults were illiterate in 2024 out of roughly 5.8 billion adults, a literacy rate near 87 percent, against an estimated 1-5 percent in ancient Egypt (UCL Digital Egypt).

items.bewering: Tog eet baie gesinne nog elke dag brood, en hulle speel nog bordspeletjies.
items.bron: GroundUp, 'What's up with the price of bread?' (groundup.org.za): bread is a staple for more than half of South Africa's population; Bizcommunity industry review: bread is among the five foods most commonly bought by eight in ten South African households. IMARC Group, 'Board Games Market' (imarcgroup.com): a global board-game market of about USD 20 billion in 2025, driven by play with family and friends. 'Baie' rather than 'die meeste' is the right quantifier.

items.bewering: Mense in antieke Egipte het ook brood geëet en bordspeletjies gespeel.
items.bron: Met, 'Food and Feasts in Middle Kingdom Egypt' and 'Ancient Egypt board games'. The then-and-now comparison was checked for its mapping as well: it contrasts schooling and literacy (consistent with 'Net sommige kinders het skoolgegaan' and 'Min mense kon lees en skryf' earlier) and links bread and board games (both supported). A learner reasoning further is not led anywhere false.

items.bewering: stapelvoedsel: Die gewone kos wat mense byna elke dag eet of drink.
items.bron: Afrikaans Wikipedia, 'Stapelvoedsel': 'n soort kos wat daagliks in sulke hoeveelhede geëet word dat dit 'n oorheersende deel van 'n standaarddieet uitmaak en 'n groot deel van die energiebehoeftes verskaf. FAO AGROVOC thesaurus, 'staple foods': foods eaten regularly and in such quantities as to constitute the dominant part of the diet and supply a major proportion of total dietary energy. National Geographic: a food that makes up the dominant part of a population's diet. Every standard definition turns on the food being the MAIN part of the diet; the lesson's definition leaves that out. Read on its own, as a glossary entry is, it makes anything eaten or drunk almost daily a staple: salt, sugar, tea or coffee would all qualify, and none is a staple.
items.regstelling: The definition must carry the defining element: a staple is the main food that makes up most of what people eat, not simply something they eat or drink every day. Something in the sense of 'Die hoofkos wat mense byna elke dag eet en wat die grootste deel van hulle kos uitmaak.' Because the lesson calls beer a staple, the writer may keep 'of drink' as long as the 'main part of the diet' element is present; beer counted as a staple in ancient Egypt because it was a primary source of nourishment, not because it was drunk daily.

items.bewering: linne: 'n Stof wat van die vesels in die stingels van die vlasplant geweef word.
items.bron: Encyclopedia.com, 'Cloth Production', and Karen Finch Textiles lecture 'Linen' (karenfinchtextiles.com/lecture/linen): linen is woven from bast fibres separated from the stem of the flax plant and spun into thread. True read on its own.

items.bewering: vakman: 'n Bekwame werker wat dinge met die hand maak, soos potte, meubels en juwele.
items.bron: Wiktionary 'vakman' (craftsman, ambachtsman) and Dutch dictionary entries giving 'geschoold ambachtsman'; the craftsmen of Deir el-Medina (carpenters, potters, metalworkers, jewellers). No online Afrikaans dictionary entry could be reached. In modern Afrikaans 'vakman' is also used for tradesmen such as plumbers and electricians who do not chiefly make things; read alone the entry is therefore narrower than the word, but it is not false, and it fits the lesson's use.

items.bewering: senet: 'n Antieke Egiptiese bordspeletjie waarin twee spelers stukke oor 'n bord skuif.
items.bron: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Ancient Egypt board games' and 'Board Games from Ancient Egypt and the Near East': a two-player game on a 30-square board, pieces moved by throws of casting sticks.

items.bewering: mummifisering: Die uitdroog en toedraai van 'n dooie liggaam om dit te bewaar.
items.bron: Smithsonian, 'Ask Smithsonian: How do you make a mummy?' (smithsonianmag.com) and si.edu 'Mummies' spotlight; Australian Museum, 'How were ancient Egyptians mummified?': the body was dried with natron, for about 40 days, then wrapped in linen to preserve it. The removal of organs is left out, which is a simplification rather than an error, and 'n dooie liggaam' correctly covers animal mummies too.

items.bewering: offer: Iets soos kos of drinkgoed wat mense aan 'n god gee.
items.bron: Wikipedia, 'Ancient Egyptian offerings', citing UCL Digital Egypt 'Daily cult' and Ockinga in Redford (2001): food, drink, clothing and ointment were offered to deities, by priests daily and by individuals privately. Egyptians also gave food and drink offerings to the dead at tombs; the entry does not mention this, which is an omission and not a falsehood, and 'Iets soos' leaves room for objects.

items.bewering: amulet: 'n Klein voorwerp wat mense gedra het om hulle teen kwaad te beskerm.
items.bron: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'Ancient Egyptian Amulets' (Heilbrunn Timeline): miniature representations of animals, deities, symbols or objects; Johns Hopkins Archaeological Museum: worn for protection by the living and placed on the dead. Note only: the past tense 'gedra het' reads as if amulets belong only to the past, which is not quite so, but the entry is not false.

items.bewering: skrifgeleerde: Iemand wie se werk dit was om te lees, te skryf en rekords te hou.
items.bron: UCL Digital Egypt, 'Literacy', and Zinn, 'Education, Pharaonic Egypt': scribes were the literate officials of Egypt; state scribes kept tax, ration and labour records and recorded legal transactions (also the Egyptian Museum statue of the scribe Hapy reading a papyrus, egypt-museum.com).

opsomming: Every claim about daily life, food, clothing, gods, schooling and the then-and-now comparison checks out against museum and university sources, but the glossary entry for 'stapelvoedsel' leaves out that a staple is the MAIN part of the diet, so read on its own it would make salt, sugar or tea a staple and must be narrowed.
